BibTex:
@article{scheibler2024lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing,
    author = "Scheibler, Jakob and Kosmehl, Alina Sabine and Studnitzky, Thomas and Zhong, Chongliang and Weißgärber, Thomas",
    title = "Lithography-Based Metal Manufacturing of Copper: Influence of Exposure Parameters on Green Part Strength",
    year = "2024",
    journal = "Metals",
    volume = "14",
    pages = "1268",
    month = "Nov",
    doi = "10.3390/met14111268",
    url = "https://doi.org/10.3390/met14111268",
    publisher = "MDPI AG",
    issue = "11",
    issn = "2075-4701"
}


Abstract:
Copper’s high thermal and electrical conductivity enables its application in heat exchangers and high-frequency components. For those applications, additive manufacturing has advantages with respect to functional integration, miniaturization, and reduced waste. However, the processing of copper is a challenge for established laser-based processes since copper’s high reflectivity impedes energy input. Sinter-based additive manufacturing processes do not exhibit this limitation since the energy for the fusion of material is applied by thermal energy during sintering. This makes them an ideal candidate for copper manufacturing. In the following work, Lithography-based Metal Manufacturing (LMM) of copper is demonstrated. Curing behavior is investigated by single-layer exposure (SLE) tests measuring curing thickness for different loading factors, particle sizes, and exposure times. Bending strength is investigated as a function of exposure time, loading factor, and orientation in the building space. A higher exposure time and lower loading factors increase bending strength. Furthermore, samples with different loading factors are produced to measure the impact of the loading factor on sintered density. For these parameters, no clear trend is demonstrated.

New Deformation Mechanisms in Nanocrystalline Nano-porous Small Scale Metals as Defined by Kinetically-driven Microstructures

The excerpt identifies DE-SC0016945 as a U.S. Department of Energy Basic Energy Sciences (DOE BES) award and provides the project title: “New Deformation Mechanisms in Nanocrystalline Nano-porous Small Scale Metals as Defined by Kinetically-driven Microstructures.” Julia R. Greer of Caltech is listed as the principal investigator. The document describes the work as a supplement supporting final research activities under Greer’s former DOE BES grant, rather than specifying a separate dollar amount, award duration, or detailed budget. The scientific scope centers on linking mechanical properties to atomic-scale and multiscale microstructure in additively manufactured nanocrystalline metals fabricated using hydrogel infusion additive manufacturing (HIAM). HIAM uses metal-ion-infused hydrogel templates and serial hydrothermal oxidation and reduction treatments to produce microscale and nanoscale Ni, Cu, and Cu-Ni materials with nanocrystallinity, nanopores, ligands, grain/twin boundaries, and unusual boundary energetics. The stated tasks were to identify processing parameters controlling grain size, pore size, and grains per ligand; determine grain-boundary energetics and ligand-size distributions through nanomechanical testing and molecular-dynamics simulations; and uncover deformation mechanisms associated with single- versus multiple-grain ligands, internal free-volume-enabled surface relaxation, and dominant grain boundaries.

The technical scope includes hydrogel-infusion-based two-photon lithography and nanoscale additive manufacturing to fabricate three-dimensional nickel nanopillars with hierarchical “bamboo-like” architectures.                    ABSTRACT


Electrode structure is closely coupled with mechanical behavior, ion transport, and reaction

uniformity during battery operation. In addition to conventional slurry-cast electrodes,

emerging fabrication approaches provide new opportunities to study and design electrode

architectures.  This  thesis  investigates  lithium-ion  battery  electrodes  through  two

complementary perspectives related to the electrode structure: micro-scale mechanical

characterization to elucidate degradation mechanisms and additive manufacturing of three-

dimensional  (3D)   micro-architected   electrodes   to   investigate   structure-transport

relationships.


In Chapters 2 and 3, the mechanical behavior of lithium-ion battery electrodes was

investigated using nanoindentation and micro-pillar compression experiments. State-of-

charge-dependent mechanical properties of electroplated LiCoO2 (LCO) cathodes were

quantified, revealing a decreasing tendency  in  elastic modulus and hardness during

delithiation, which  is attributed to the expansion of LCO layered structure. Fracture

toughness distribution across the electrode thickness was analyzed to understand how

structural heterogeneity contributes to the mechanical property landscape. In addition, we

studied the deformation of lithium-based composite anodes, confirming that the Li/Na

composite anode exhibits higher deformability at the electrode-electrolyte interface, which

enhances interfacial contact.


The interconnected pore structure and large surface-to-volume ratio of 3D architected battery

electrodes render them promising for enhancing electrochemical performance via more

efficient ionic transport. In Chapters 4 and 5, we develop a hydrogel infusion additive

manufacturing (HIAM)-based approach to fabricate micro-architected LiFePO4 (LFP)/C

composite electrodes with feature sizes down to 18 µm. The concomitant formation of carbon

within the lattice enhances the mechanical strength, which preserves shape integrity of the

3D structure during cell assembly and function. We designed electrodes with different

geometries, including  tilted cubes, honeycombs, and triply periodic minimal surfaces

(TPMS), to probe the influence of geometric factors on electrochemical performance under                                                                            v
various charge-discharge rates. We propose an experimentally informed electrochemical
model that demonstrates the roles of Li+ transport in the electrolyte and Li+ diffusion in the

electrode in determining the utilization of active materials. This work introduces a versatile

manufacturing platform for printing 3D battery components and provides insights into

structure optimization for high-performance rechargeable batteries.                                                                                                       vi

{"answer": "# Funding of Metal Vat Photopolymerization Research and Development

## Overview

This survey identifies the public and private funding sources that support research and development of metal vat photopolymerization (VP)—including sinter-based metal DLP/stereolithography with powder-loaded photoresins, lithography-based metal manufacturing (LMM), metal-ion/metal-salt photoresins, hydrogel infusion additive manufacturing (HIAM), and two-photon lithography (TPL) routes that yield metal or metal-oxide parts after calcination, reduction, debinding, or sintering. The analysis is based on acknowledgment sections, grant identifiers, and patent records retrieved from published literature.

The following table summarizes all identified funding relationships:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## 1. U.S. Department of Energy (DOE): The Dominant Funder

The DOE Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences (BES), is the single most prominent funder of metal VP research identified in this survey. The flagship grant is **DE-SC0016945**, awarded to **Julia R. Greer** (PI) at the California Institute of Technology, with the project title "New Deformation Mechanisms in Nanocrystalline Nano-porous Small Scale Metals as Defined by Kinetically-driven Microstructures" (pqac-00000018). This BES award has supported the development of hydrogel infusion additive manufacturing (HIAM) for Cu, Ni, Ag, Cu-Ni, and multicomponent alloys, as well as two-photon-lithography/HIAM fabrication of Ni nanopillars (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000021). The same grant number appears in the acknowledgments of the seminal Saccone et al. 2022 *Nature* paper ("This work was supported by the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences, under Award No. DE-SC0016945") (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002), the corresponding preprint (pqac-00000020), the Greer 2025 DOE final report (pqac-00000018), and the Serles et al. 2026 *Nature Reviews Materials* review (pqac-00000022).

At **Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL)**, the work of Yaw et al. Context. We are a university alloy-development lab (laser powder bed fusion of Al-Zr and Al-Mn-Cr-Zr
alloys, a Cu-Cr-Zr complement, and our own ultrasonic atomization of powder). We are evaluating
sinter-based metal vat photopolymerization: metal powder (usually MIM grade, D50 under ~20 um, about
45-60 vol%) in a light-curable binder is cured layer by layer by DLP or laser stereolithography, and
the green part is cleaned, debound and sintered as in metal injection molding (MIM). Examples:
Holo Inc.'s PureForm (2017-2024; pure copper above 92% IACS, then stainless steel), whose assets
Greene Group Industries, a US MIM contract manufacturer, bought in March 2024 and now sells as a
parts service in 17-4PH and 316 (film-fed bottom-up DLP; design guide: 0.07 mm minimum wall, 3.5 mm
maximum wall, +/-0.025 mm up to 12 mm, 0.8-1.6 um Ra as printed); Incus GmbH's Lithography-based
Metal Manufacturing (LMM; Hammer printers; steels, Ti-6Al-4V, 99.9% Cu, precious metals); and
Admatec's Admaflex DLP. Adjacent routes that make metal through a photopolymer step (Caltech's
hydrogel infusion AM, metal-organic or metal-ion photoresins, two-photon lithography) count too.
Generic polymer or ceramic vat photopolymerization is out of scope except where it informs metal
parts.

Question. Who funds research and development of metal vat photopolymerization? In scope: DLP,
stereolithography, LMM or two-photon lithography that ends in metal parts (photocurable metal-powder
slurries that are debound and sintered; metal-ion, metal-salt or metal-organic photoresins and
hydrogel infusion that are calcined and reduced to metal). Out of scope: polymer-only or
ceramic-only vat photopolymerization, and polymer lattices that are only electroplated. For each
paper or project give the agency and program (for example NSF CMMI, NSF SBIR/STTR, DOE Office of
Science BES, DOE AMMTO or AMO, ARPA-E, ONR, AFOSR, ARO, AFRL, DARPA, NASA, NIH, NIST), the grant or
contract number exactly as acknowledged, the principal investigator and institution or company, the
year, and the metal. Include company awards (for example to Holo Inc.) and US national-lab programs
(LLNL, ORNL, Sandia, ARL, AFRL) where they appear, and the non-US public funders (EU Horizon, the
Austrian FFG for Incus or TU Wien, Fraunhofer) for comparison. Quote the acknowledgment sentence where
you can, and say which agencies and program areas fund the most of this work.

Based on the evidence retrieved, the **DOE Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences** program is the most prolific single funder of metal VP research, primarily through grant DE-SC0016945 to the Greer group at Caltech, which has generated the majority of high-impact publications in this space (the 2022 *Nature* paper with 258 citations, the 2026 *Nature Reviews Materials* review, and multiple theses and DOE reports). Austrian public funding for Incus or TU Wien LMM metal research was not identified in the documents retrieved, suggesting that much of the Austrian LMM development may be commercially funded by Incus GmbH and its predecessor Lithoz.

**NSF** appears modestly in the form of a graduate fellowship supporting the MIT ImpFab work. No NSF CMMI, NSF SBIR/STTR, DARPA, ARPA-E, NASA, AFOSR, or NIST awards were specifically identified as funding metal VP research in the retrieved literature, though this absence may reflect limitations in the search rather than a true absence of such awards. In particular, the Nguyen and Chung group at Michigan State University has published on photopolymerization of stainless steel 420 metal suspensions (cited in the Mastny thesis as reference 18), but their funding acknowledgments were not retrievable in this search.

This survey is based on papers, patents, and reports retrievable through academic databases and patent search systems. It may not capture all relevant SBIR/STTR awards (which are often disclosed in federal award databases like SBIR.gov rather than in patent texts), classified or ITAR-restricted programs, or industry-funded work where acknowledgments are omitted. The question of Austrian FFG funding for Incus/TU Wien LMM work remains open; such grants may exist in Austrian funding databases but were not found in the English-language academic literature retrieved here.

- **European Regional Development Fund (ERDF/EFRE)**: The Scheibler et al. 2024 study on LMM of copper at the Fraunhofer Institute for Ceramic Technologies and Systems (Fraunhofer IKTS, Germany) was funded by the ERDF through the **AddiMet** project (funding reference **100405446**), with co-financing from tax revenues of the Free State of Saxony (pqac-00000014).

- **TU Wien / Incus GmbH (Austria)**: The Mastny 2026 thesis at TU Wien, which used an Incus LMM printer for copper alloy (Ag and Cu-Sn bronze) feedstock development, did not identify any external government grants or Austrian FFG funding in its acknowledgments. The thesis was supervised by Christian Gierl-Mayer and Atul Anand at TU Wien's Institute for Chemical Technologies and Analytics, Powder Metallurgy division (pqac-00000010). This suggests the work may have been internally funded or supported by industry collaboration with Incus GmbH, whose commercial LMM platform (the Hammer series) was used.

- **Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC)** and the **Swiss ETH Domain Strategic Focus Area—Additive Manufacturing Program** are acknowledged in the Serles et al. 2026 *Nature Reviews Materials* review, along with the Schmidt Science Fellowship and Rhodes Trust (pqac-00000022).

- **Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST)**, South Korea (grant **CG2014**), co-funded the Yee et al. 2019 Caltech two-photon lithography work (pqac-00000009).

## 6. Company-Associated Work

- **Holo Inc.** (Oakland, CA): Multiple patents were identified (US10245785B2, US10464259B2, US11351735B2, US11945166B2) assigned to Holo Inc. and invented by Brian Adzima, Pierre Lin, Richard M. Greene, and Viswanath Meenakshisundaram (pqac-00000015). No government funding statements (such as SBIR/STTR rights notices) were found in the retrieved patent records. Holo appears to have been primarily venture-funded. Its assets were acquired by Greene Group Industries in March 2024.

- **Xiangjia Li / Arizona State University**: Patent US20250222650A1 describes a metal-salt photocurable resin system for continuous DLP fabrication of copper objects from CuSO₄-loaded photoresins. The patent was filed by Xiangjia Li and Dylan Joralmon with Arizona State University as current assignee (pqac-00000016). No government funding statement was found in the patent text.

## 7. Which Agencies and Programs Fund the Most

Based on the evidence retrieved, the **DOE Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences** program is the most prolific single funder of metal VP research, primarily through grant DE-SC0016945 to the Greer group at Caltech, which has generated the majority of high-impact publications in this space (the 2022 *Nature* paper with 258 citations, the 2026 *Nature Reviews Materials* review, and multiple theses and DOE reports). DOE also funds the LLNL HIAM program via the laboratory operating contract.

The **DoD** complex (ONR, ARL/ARO, and the Vannevar Bush Fellowship) collectively constitutes the second largest U.S. public funder, supporting both the MIT ImpFab work and Caltech metallo-polyelectrolyte and two-photon lithography projects. **NIH** provides significant co-funding, particularly for the MIT and Caltech projects, often through training grants and neuroscience/biomedical mechanism awards.

In Europe, the **EU ERDF** (via German state co-financing) supports LMM copper development at Fraunhofer IKTS. Austrian public funding for Incus or TU Wien LMM metal research was not identified in the documents retrieved, suggesting that much of the Austrian LMM development may be commercially funded by Incus GmbH and its predecessor Lithoz.

**NSF** appears modestly in the form of a graduate fellowship supporting the MIT ImpFab work. No NSF CMMI, NSF SBIR/STTR, DARPA, ARPA-E, NASA, AFOSR, or NIST awards were specifically identified as funding metal VP research in the retrieved literature, though this absence may reflect limitations in the search rather than a true absence of such awards. In particular, the Nguyen and Chung group at Michigan State University has published on photopolymerization of stainless steel 420 metal suspensions (cited in the Mastny thesis as reference 18), but their funding acknowledgments were not retrievable in this search.

## Caveats

This survey is based on papers, patents, and reports retrievable through academic databases and patent search systems. It may not capture all relevant SBIR/STTR awards (which are often disclosed in federal award databases like SBIR.gov rather than in patent texts), classified or ITAR-restricted programs, or industry-funded work where acknowledgments are omitted. The question of Austrian FFG funding for Incus/TU Wien LMM work remains open; such grants may exist in Austrian funding databases but were not found in the English-language academic literature retrieved here.

contexts.question:
Context. We are a university alloy-development lab (laser powder bed fusion of Al-Zr and Al-Mn-Cr-Zr
alloys, a Cu-Cr-Zr complement, and our own ultrasonic atomization of powder). We are evaluating
sinter-based metal vat photopolymerization: metal powder (usually MIM grade, D50 under ~20 um, about
45-60 vol%) in a light-curable binder is cured layer by layer by DLP or laser stereolithography, and
the green part is cleaned, debound and sintered as in metal injection molding (MIM). Examples:
Holo Inc.'s PureForm (2017-2024; pure copper above 92% IACS, then stainless steel), whose assets
Greene Group Industries, a US MIM contract manufacturer, bought in March 2024 and now sells as a
parts service in 17-4PH and 316 (film-fed bottom-up DLP; design guide: 0.07 mm minimum wall, 3.5 mm
maximum wall, +/-0.025 mm up to 12 mm, 0.8-1.6 um Ra as printed); Incus GmbH's Lithography-based
Metal Manufacturing (LMM; Hammer printers; steels, Ti-6Al-4V, 99.9% Cu, precious metals); and
Admatec's Admaflex DLP. Adjacent routes that make metal through a photopolymer step (Caltech's
hydrogel infusion AM, metal-organic or metal-ion photoresins, two-photon lithography) count too.
Generic polymer or ceramic vat photopolymerization is out of scope except where it informs metal
parts.

Question. Who funds research and development of metal vat photopolymerization? In scope: DLP,
stereolithography, LMM or two-photon lithography that ends in metal parts (photocurable metal-powder
slurries that are debound and sintered; metal-ion, metal-salt or metal-organic photoresins and
hydrogel infusion that are calcined and reduced to metal). Out of scope: polymer-only or
ceramic-only vat photopolymerization, and polymer lattices that are only electroplated. For each
paper or project give the agency and program (for example NSF CMMI, NSF SBIR/STTR, DOE Office of
Science BES, DOE AMMTO or AMO, ARPA-E, ONR, AFOSR, ARO, AFRL, DARPA, NASA, NIH, NIST), the grant or
contract number exactly as acknowledged, the principal investigator and institution or company, the
year, and the metal. Include company awards (for example to Holo Inc.) and US national-lab programs
(LLNL, ORNL, Sandia, ARL, AFRL) where they appear, and the non-US public funders (EU Horizon, the
Austrian FFG for Incus or TU Wien, Fraunhofer) for comparison. Quote the acknowledgment sentence where
you can, and say which agencies and program areas fund the most of this work.

the green part is cleaned, debound and sintered as in metal injection molding (MIM). Examples:

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies Julia R. Greer as the principal investigator and describes research broadly consistent with a DOE BES project on deformation mechanisms in nanocrystalline, nanoporous small-scale metals. The technical scope includes hydrogel-infusion-based two-photon lithography and nanoscale additive manufacturing to fabricate three-dimensional nickel nanopillars with hierarchical “bamboo-like” architectures. These structures contain approximately 30–50 nm grains, similarly scaled pores, and tunable final diameters of roughly 130–550 nm. The work combines customized photoresists, hydrogel templating, nickel nitrate infusion, calcination, forming-gas reduction, high-resolution TEM/SEM characterization, in situ uniaxial compression, and atomistic molecular-dynamics simulations. Reported outcomes include strengths of 1–3 GPa, a suppressed small-pillar size effect with approximate scaling σ ∝ D⁻⁰.², and a transition from localized shear banding in smaller pillars to more distributed plasticity in larger pillars. The excerpt also indicates DOE-supported results involving PhD students Wenxin Zhang and Thomas Tran. However, it does not provide the full grant title or scope as an official award description, award dates, funding amount, budget breakdown, institutional co-investigators, or explicit details tying grant number DE-SC0016945 to the project.

snippets: New Deformation Mechanisms in Nanocrystalline Nano-porous Small Scale Metals as Defined by Kinetically-driven Microstructures
Julia R Greer, PI
This report describes recent advances in the design and fabrication of nanostructured metallic pillars with hierarchical microstructures using a novel nanoscale additive manufacturing approach.
Through a hydrogel-infusion-based two-photon lithography (TPL) method, we successfully fabricated 3D nickel nanopillars exhibiting both nanocrystalline and nanoporous features.
Wenxin Zhang, supported PhD student
Presented results supported by the DOE

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies DE-SC0016945 as a U.S. Department of Energy Basic Energy Sciences (DOE BES) award and provides the project title: “New Deformation Mechanisms in Nanocrystalline Nano-porous Small Scale Metals as Defined by Kinetically-driven Microstructures.” Julia R. Greer of Caltech is listed as the principal investigator. The document describes the work as a supplement supporting final research activities under Greer’s former DOE BES grant, rather than specifying a separate dollar amount, award duration, or detailed budget. The scientific scope centers on linking mechanical properties to atomic-scale and multiscale microstructure in additively manufactured nanocrystalline metals fabricated using hydrogel infusion additive manufacturing (HIAM). HIAM uses metal-ion-infused hydrogel templates and serial hydrothermal oxidation and reduction treatments to produce microscale and nanoscale Ni, Cu, and Cu-Ni materials with nanocrystallinity, nanopores, ligands, grain/twin boundaries, and unusual boundary energetics. The stated tasks were to identify processing parameters controlling grain size, pore size, and grains per ligand; determine grain-boundary energetics and ligand-size distributions through nanomechanical testing and molecular-dynamics simulations; and uncover deformation mechanisms associated with single- versus multiple-grain ligands, internal free-volume-enabled surface relaxation, and dominant grain boundaries.

contexts.question:
Context. We are a university alloy-development lab (laser powder bed fusion of Al-Zr and Al-Mn-Cr-Zr
alloys, a Cu-Cr-Zr complement, and our own ultrasonic atomization of powder). We are evaluating
sinter-based metal vat photopolymerization: metal powder (usually MIM grade, D50 under ~20 um, about
45-60 vol%) in a light-curable binder is cured layer by layer by DLP or laser stereolithography, and
the green part is cleaned, debound and sintered as in metal injection molding (MIM). Examples:
Holo Inc.'s PureForm (2017-2024; pure copper above 92% IACS, then stainless steel), whose assets
Greene Group Industries, a US MIM contract manufacturer, bought in March 2024 and now sells as a
parts service in 17-4PH and 316 (film-fed bottom-up DLP; design guide: 0.07 mm minimum wall, 3.5 mm
maximum wall, +/-0.025 mm up to 12 mm, 0.8-1.6 um Ra as printed); Incus GmbH's Lithography-based
Metal Manufacturing (LMM; Hammer printers; steels, Ti-6Al-4V, 99.9% Cu, precious metals); and
Admatec's Admaflex DLP. Adjacent routes that make metal through a photopolymer step (Caltech's
hydrogel infusion AM, metal-organic or metal-ion photoresins, two-photon lithography) count too.
Generic polymer or ceramic vat photopolymerization is out of scope except where it informs metal
parts.

Question. Who funds research and development of metal vat photopolymerization? In scope: DLP,
stereolithography, LMM or two-photon lithography that ends in metal parts (photocurable metal-powder
slurries that are debound and sintered; metal-ion, metal-salt or metal-organic photoresins and
hydrogel infusion that are calcined and reduced to metal). Out of scope: polymer-only or
ceramic-only vat photopolymerization, and polymer lattices that are only electroplated. For each
paper or project give the agency and program (for example NSF CMMI, NSF SBIR/STTR, DOE Office of
Science BES, DOE AMMTO or AMO, ARPA-E, ONR, AFOSR, ARO, AFRL, DARPA, NASA, NIH, NIST), the grant or

# Funding of Metal Vat Photopolymerization Research and Development

## Overview

This survey identifies the public and private funding sources that support research and development of metal vat photopolymerization (VP)—including sinter-based metal DLP/stereolithography with powder-loaded photoresins, lithography-based metal manufacturing (LMM), metal-ion/metal-salt photoresins, hydrogel infusion additive manufacturing (HIAM), and two-photon lithography (TPL) routes that yield metal or metal-oxide parts after calcination, reduction, debinding, or sintering. The analysis is based on acknowledgment sections, grant identifiers, and patent records retrieved from published literature.

*Table: Funding agencies, programs, exact award identifiers, investigators, institutions and material endpoints found for metal vat-photopolymerization and closely related photochemical metal-manufacturing projects. Rows distinguish confirmed public funding from projects whose retrieved records state no external award.*

## 1. U.S. Department of Energy (DOE): The Dominant Funder

The DOE Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences (BES), is the single most prominent funder of metal VP research identified in this survey. The flagship grant is **DE-SC0016945**, awarded to **Julia R. Greer** (PI) at the California Institute of Technology, with the project title "New Deformation Mechanisms in Nanocrystalline Nano-porous Small Scale Metals as Defined by Kinetically-driven Microstructures" (greer2025newdeformationmechanisms pages 1-4). This BES award has supported the development of hydrogel infusion additive manufacturing (HIAM) for Cu, Ni, Ag, Cu-Ni, and multicomponent alloys, as well as two-photon-lithography/HIAM fabrication of Ni nanopillars (saccone2022additivemanufacturingof pages 7-8, greer2025newdeformationmechanisms pages 4-8). The same grant number appears in the acknowledgments of the seminal Saccone et al. 2022 *Nature* paper ("This work was supported by the U.S. Department of Energy, Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences, under Award No. DE-SC0016945") (saccone2022microscalefabricationof pages 9-12), the corresponding preprint (saccone2022microscalefabricationof pages 9-12), the Greer 2025 DOE final report (greer2025newdeformationmechanisms pages 1-4), and the Serles et al. 2026 *Nature Reviews Materials* review (serles2026nanoscaleadditivemanufacturing pages 20-21).

At **Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL)**, the work of Yaw et al. (2025) on precursor design for HIAM of ceramics (including CuO and ZrO₂) was "performed under the auspices of the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) by the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) under Contract No. **DE-AC52-07NA27344**" (yaw2025precursordesignfor pages 16-17). A graduate fellowship from the DOE **University Nuclear Leadership Program** (grant **DE_NE0009089**) also supported this LLNL work (yaw2025precursordesignfor pages 16-17). While the Yaw et al. study focused on ceramic endpoints, the authors explicitly developed HIAM process knowledge directly applicable to metal fabrication.

## 2. U.S. Department of Defense (DoD)

Multiple DoD agencies appear in the acknowledgments of metal VP publications:

- **Office of Naval Research (ONR)**: Grant **N00014-17-1-2977** supported the Oran et al. 2018 *Science* paper on Implosion Fabrication (ImpFab) at MIT (PI: Edward S. Boyden), which demonstrated volumetric silver deposition in photopatterned hydrogel scaffolds followed by dehydration-induced shrinkage to nanoscale features (oran20183dnanofabricationby pages 3-5).

- **U.S. Army Research Laboratory and Army Research Office (ARL/ARO)**: Contract **W911NF1510548** co-funded the same Oran/Boyden ImpFab project (oran20183dnanofabricationby pages 3-5). Separately, ARO contract **W911NF-19-D-0001** supported the Lee et al. 2024 *Nature Communications* work at Caltech on stereolithography-printed metallo-polyelectrolyte gels via the Institute for Collaborative Biotechnologies (lee2024molecularcontrolvia pages 11-11).

- **DoD Vannevar Bush Faculty Fellowship**: Acknowledged in the Yee et al. 2019 *Advanced Materials* paper (Caltech, PI: Julia R. Greer) on two-photon lithography of zinc-ion photoresins to produce 3D-architected ZnO nanostructures, though no specific fellowship number was stated (yee2019additivemanufacturingof pages 7-8).

## 3. National Institutes of Health (NIH)

NIH grants appear in multiple metal VP projects:

- **1R01CA194533** supported the Yee et al. 2019 Caltech two-photon lithography/photopolymer-complex-synthesis work on ZnO architectures (yee2019additivemanufacturingof pages 7-8).
- **T32GM112592** (NIH Biotechnology Leadership Training Program) also supported the same Yee et al. 2019 study (yee2019additivemanufacturingof pages 7-8).
- Multiple NIH grants supported the Boyden/MIT ImpFab silver work: **1R01EB024261**, **1U01MH106011**, **1DP1NS087724** (NIH Director's Pioneer Award), **1R01MH103910**, **2R01DA029639**, **1RM1HG008525**, and **1R24MH106075** (oran20183dnanofabricationby pages 3-5).

## 4. National Science Foundation (NSF)

The NSF **Graduate Research Fellowship Program** (award **1122374**) supported Samuel G. Rodriques on the Oran et al. 2018 ImpFab project at MIT (oran20183dnanofabricationby pages 3-5, oran20183dnanofabricationby pages 5-5). No direct NSF research grants (e.g., NSF CMMI or NSF SBIR/STTR) were identified in the retrieved metal VP literature, though this may reflect incomplete coverage of all published work in this field.

## 5. European and Non-US Public Funders

- **European Regional Development Fund (ERDF/EFRE)**: The Scheibler et al. 2024 study on LMM of copper at the Fraunhofer Institute for Ceramic Technologies and Systems (Fraunhofer IKTS, Germany) was funded by the ERDF through the **AddiMet** project (funding reference **100405446**), with co-financing from tax revenues of the Free State of Saxony (scheibler2024lithographybasedmetalmanufacturing pages 15-17).

- **TU Wien / Incus GmbH (Austria)**: The Mastny 2026 thesis at TU Wien, which used an Incus LMM printer for copper alloy (Ag and Cu-Sn bronze) feedstock development, did not identify any external government grants or Austrian FFG funding in its acknowledgments. The thesis was supervised by Christian Gierl-Mayer and Atul Anand at TU Wien's Institute for Chemical Technologies and Analytics, Powder Metallurgy division (mastny2026highstrengthcopperalloys pages 1-5). This suggests the work may have been internally funded or supported by industry collaboration with Incus GmbH, whose commercial LMM platform (the Hammer series) was used.

- **Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC)** and the **Swiss ETH Domain Strategic Focus Area—Additive Manufacturing Program** are acknowledged in the Serles et al. 2026 *Nature Reviews Materials* review, along with the Schmidt Science Fellowship and Rhodes Trust (serles2026nanoscaleadditivemanufacturing pages 20-21).

- **Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST)**, South Korea (grant **CG2014**), co-funded the Yee et al. 2019 Caltech two-photon lithography work (yee2019additivemanufacturingof pages 7-8).

## 6. Company-Associated Work

- **Holo Inc.** (Oakland, CA): Multiple patents were identified (US10245785B2, US10464259B2, US11351735B2, US11945166B2) assigned to Holo Inc. and invented by Brian Adzima, Pierre Lin, Richard M. Greene, and Viswanath Meenakshisundaram (US10245785B2 pages 1-2). No government funding statements (such as SBIR/STTR rights notices) were found in the retrieved patent records. Holo appears to have been primarily venture-funded. Its assets were acquired by Greene Group Industries in March 2024.

- **Xiangjia Li / Arizona State University**: Patent US20250222650A1 describes a metal-salt photocurable resin system for continuous DLP fabrication of copper objects from CuSO₄-loaded photoresins. The patent was filed by Xiangjia Li and Dylan Joralmon with Arizona State University as current assignee (US20250222650A1 pages 1-4). No government funding statement was found in the patent text.

## 7. Which Agencies and Programs Fund the Most

Based on the evidence retrieved, the **DOE Office of Science, Basic Energy Sciences** program is the most prolific single funder of metal VP research, primarily through grant DE-SC0016945 to the Greer group at Caltech, which has generated the majority of high-impact publications in this space (the 2022 *Nature* paper with 258 citations, the 2026 *Nature Reviews Materials* review, and multiple theses and DOE reports). DOE also funds the LLNL HIAM program via the laboratory operating contract.

The **DoD** complex (ONR, ARL/ARO, and the Vannevar Bush Fellowship) collectively constitutes the second largest U.S. public funder, supporting both the MIT ImpFab work and Caltech metallo-polyelectrolyte and two-photon lithography projects. **NIH** provides significant co-funding, particularly for the MIT and Caltech projects, often through training grants and neuroscience/biomedical mechanism awards.

In Europe, the **EU ERDF** (via German state co-financing) supports LMM copper development at Fraunhofer IKTS. Austrian public funding for Incus or TU Wien LMM metal research was not identified in the documents retrieved, suggesting that much of the Austrian LMM development may be commercially funded by Incus GmbH and its predecessor Lithoz.

**NSF** appears modestly in the form of a graduate fellowship supporting the MIT ImpFab work. No NSF CMMI, NSF SBIR/STTR, DARPA, ARPA-E, NASA, AFOSR, or NIST awards were specifically identified as funding metal VP research in the retrieved literature, though this absence may reflect limitations in the search rather than a true absence of such awards. In particular, the Nguyen and Chung group at Michigan State University has published on photopolymerization of stainless steel 420 metal suspensions (cited in the Mastny thesis as reference 18), but their funding acknowledgments were not retrievable in this search.

## Caveats

This survey is based on papers, patents, and reports retrievable through academic databases and patent search systems. It may not capture all relevant SBIR/STTR awards (which are often disclosed in federal award databases like SBIR.gov rather than in patent texts), classified or ITAR-restricted programs, or industry-funded work where acknowledgments are omitted. The question of Austrian FFG funding for Incus/TU Wien LMM work remains open; such grants may exist in Austrian funding databases but were not found in the English-language academic literature retrieved here.

info.query:
Context. We are a university alloy-development lab (laser powder bed fusion of Al-Zr and Al-Mn-Cr-Zr
alloys, a Cu-Cr-Zr complement, and our own ultrasonic atomization of powder). We are evaluating
sinter-based metal vat photopolymerization: metal powder (usually MIM grade, D50 under ~20 um, about
45-60 vol%) in a light-curable binder is cured layer by layer by DLP or laser stereolithography, and
the green part is cleaned, debound and sintered as in metal injection molding (MIM). Examples:
Holo Inc.'s PureForm (2017-2024; pure copper above 92% IACS, then stainless steel), whose assets
Greene Group Industries, a US MIM contract manufacturer, bought in March 2024 and now sells as a
parts service in 17-4PH and 316 (film-fed bottom-up DLP; design guide: 0.07 mm minimum wall, 3.5 mm
maximum wall, +/-0.025 mm up to 12 mm, 0.8-1.6 um Ra as printed); Incus GmbH's Lithography-based
Metal Manufacturing (LMM; Hammer printers; steels, Ti-6Al-4V, 99.9% Cu, precious metals); and
Admatec's Admaflex DLP. Adjacent routes that make metal through a photopolymer step (Caltech's
hydrogel infusion AM, metal-organic or metal-ion photoresins, two-photon lithography) count too.
Generic polymer or ceramic vat photopolymerization is out of scope except where it informs metal
parts.

Question. Who funds research and development of metal vat photopolymerization? In scope: DLP,
stereolithography, LMM or two-photon lithography that ends in metal parts (photocurable metal-powder
slurries that are debound and sintered; metal-ion, metal-salt or metal-organic photoresins and
hydrogel infusion that are calcined and reduced to metal). Out of scope: polymer-only or
ceramic-only vat photopolymerization, and polymer lattices that are only electroplated. For each
paper or project give the agency and program (for example NSF CMMI, NSF SBIR/STTR, DOE Office of
Science BES, DOE AMMTO or AMO, ARPA-E, ONR, AFOSR, ARO, AFRL, DARPA, NASA, NIH, NIST), the grant or
contract number exactly as acknowledged, the principal investigator and institution or company, the
year, and the metal. Include company awards (for example to Holo Inc.) and US national-lab programs
(LLNL, ORNL, Sandia, ARL, AFRL) where they appear, and the non-US public funders (EU Horizon, the
Austrian FFG for Incus or TU Wien, Fraunhofer) for comparison. Quote the acknowledgment sentence where
you can, and say which agencies and program areas fund the most of this work.
